title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: A Review

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Wearable and Computational EEG Advances for Rehabilitation Monitoring
subsections.content: Brain imaging is an important achievement of modern science, and it is thriving. With the improvement of temporal and spatial resolution of brain imaging techniques, as well as the integration of multimodal imaging methods, the observation scale of the brain is becoming wider, which is conducive to the research of brain science and the treatment of brain diseases. This section introduces the application of EEG, MEG, fMRI, fNIRS, and multimodal imaging in the motor function assessment of stroke, with particular relevance to recent wearable EEG hardware, computational EEG analysis, rehabilitation monitoring, and motor performance prediction ref [1], ref [2], ref [3], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6]. Fig. 1 shows the equipment for the four imaging modalities and the preliminary visualization results of the collected data.

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: MEG Biomarkers of Motor Network Dysfunction and Recovery
subsections.content: EEG is a general reflection of the electrical activity of brain nerve cells in the scalp ref [27]. With a time resolution of milliseconds, it can record faster brain activity ref [10]. However, the spatial resolution of EEG is limited because it is necessary to place an electrode with a diameter of about 1 cm on the scalp ref [28]. With the development of high-density EEG and source location technology, EEG has shown unique advantages in the field of diagnosis and evaluation of brain diseases ref [29], ref [30]. EEG electrode positioning is based on the standard 10-20 system, which currently achieves up to 256 channels ref [31]. Before a further state analysis, source localization analysis of raw EEG signals is required, that is, inverse estimation of the location, direction, and intensity of neural activity sources in the brain. Source localization analysis software includes MATLAB plugins, such as Brainstorm, EEGLAB, FieldTrip, NutMeg, and SPM, as well as independent analysis software, such as MNE, OpenMEEG, and NeuroFEM ref [32].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy for Naturalistic Neurorehabilitation Assessment
subsections.content: MEG records neural activity by measuring changes in the brain's magnetic field using a sensitive magnetometer with a spatial resolution better than EEG [ref [7], ref [8]]. However, MEG is easily interfered with by environmental magnetic fields when measuring small magnetic field changes [ref [5]]. MEG has become a means of stroke assessment or other brain disease detection because the spatial resolution has been further improved with the increase of the number of sensors, and the source location algorithm has also been extensively developed [ref [8], ref [5]]. More than 250 channels of MEG signal can be collected simultaneously [ref [8]]. MEG and EEG are different manifestations of the same signal, so analysis software is common to both [ref [7]]. The difficulty of collecting MEG signals is that the magnetic field generated by brain activity is the pT degree, more than 100 times weaker than the Earth's magnetic field [ref [5], ref [8]]. MEG's recording was made possible by the invention of a sensitive magnetic flux detector called superconducting quantum interference device [ref [8]].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Electroencephalography for Stroke Detection, Prognosis, and Motor Assessment
subsections.content: fMRI is a nonradioactive technique that looks at brain activity based on blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) and has been widely used in neuroscience. Changes in movement-related BOLD activation patterns during stroke rehabilitation provide evidence for the use of fMRI in rehabilitation assessment, while in this subsection EEG has been widely used for stroke detection and monitoring of brain dysfunction ref [11], ref [12], ref [13]. The prediction of motor rehabilitation combined with fMRI showed an increase in explanation compared to the FMA score alone, and quantitative EEG has also shown value for predicting upper limb motor recovery ref [14]. Interhemispheric activation balance in motor-related cortex changes with the rehabilitation process and laterality indexes (LIs) before and after the improvement of motor function can be a good measurement; in EEG studies, related symmetry-based measures such as the brain symmetry index and revised brain symmetry index have been associated with stroke assessment and prognosis ref [16], ref [17], ref [18]. The equation LIs = (ipsilesional activation − contralesional activation) / (ipsilesional activation + contralesional activation). LIs range from −1 to 1, with +1 representing complete ipsilesional activation and −1 representing exclusively contralesional activation. Contralaterality index (CI) is essentially the same indicator as LIs, and its equation CI = (contralesional − ipsilesional) / (contralesional + ipsilesional), which is used in some reports. fMRI analysis in kinematics showed that a larger area of the cortex was activated when the patient performed ankle dorsal plantar-flexion movements one month after the rehabilitation evaluation. After six months of rehabilitation, the activation balance in the patient's primary motor cortex shifted to the affected hemisphere. Longitudinal evaluation of brain activation balance changes from onset to several months post-stroke by fMRI can effectively evaluate the rehabilitation therapy; similarly, EEG has been used for acute ischemic stroke detection, severity assessment, and prognosis ref [11], ref [12], ref [13], ref [15], ref [24], ref [25]. Two weeks after treatment with constraint-induced movement therapy, fMRI activation in the sensorimotor area increased significantly, and the magnitude was greater in ipsilesional than contralesional. In parallel, recent computational EEG approaches using wavelet features, FFT, PCA, k-NN, convolutional neural networks, deep belief networks, and extreme learning machine have been explored for post-stroke signal identification and stroke classification ref [19], ref [20], ref [21], ref [22], ref [23], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging Modalities for Post-Stroke Motor Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: fMRI and Connectivity-Based Mapping of Post-Stroke Motor Reorganization
subsections.content: fNIRS is an emerging brain imaging technology in recent years. Its principle is similar to fMRI, that is, neural activity in the brain can lead to changes in hemodynamics ref [94], ref [95]. Oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin in brain tissue have different absorption rates of near-infrared light to varying wavelengths of 600-900 nm, which can be deduced to the brain activity according to the Beer-Lambert law ref [96]. Furthermore, the spatial resolution of fNIRS as fMRI is far superior to that of EEG and MEG, as reflected by fMRI-based mapping of post-stroke motor reorganization and connectivity changes in longitudinal and intervention studies (ref [26], ref [27], ref [29], ref [32], ref [33], ref [35], ref [37], ref [40]). Meanwhile, the time sampling rate of fNIRS can reach about 10 Hz, which is higher than that of fMRI, whose temporal characteristics have shaped studies of motor recovery, task activation, and connectivity after stroke (ref [28], ref [30], ref [31], ref [34], ref [36], ref [38], ref [39]).

subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Neuroimaging Frameworks and Fusion Methods
subsections.content: Each imaging method has its advantages and disadvantages, and multimodal imaging can complement these advantages to provide a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of changes in brain structure and function ref [41]. We examined research reports from the last decade and found that the most popular multimodal combinations are EEG-fMRI ref [42], ref [45], ref [46] and EEG-fNIRS ref [43], ref [44]. EEG-MEG and fMRI-fNIRS combined studies have also been performed ref [44], but few studies have explored motor function assessment after stroke. EEG or MEG and EMG coupling analysis is another popular multimodal analysis method that can establish a correlation between brain activity and muscle behavior, which has unique advantages in assessing motor loss caused by abnormal neural activity after stroke. This section focuses on applying EEG-fMRI coupling, EEG-FNRIS coupling, and EEG-EMG coupling in motor function assessment of stroke.

subsections.subsection_title: EEG-fMRI and EEG-fNIRS in Stroke Rehabilitation and Neurofeedback
subsections.content: There is a certain degree of information transmission and interaction between the cerebral cortex and the muscles during limb motion ref [50], ref [51]. Corticomuscular coupling (CMC) is a quantitative assessment method that can reflect cerebral cortex information and motor muscle state ref [50], ref [51]. CMC reveals the FC between the cerebral cortex and muscles by quantifying the synchronization between EMG and EEG ref [47], ref [50], or MEG. The CMC phenomenon between the central nervous system and the periphery nervous system is essential for the neural control of movement. This functional coupling between the brain and muscle originates from the neural signal afferent and efferent process. The brain transmits control commands to the peripheral nervous system in electrical charges through interconnected synapses and neuronal cells and then controls the contraction or extension of various muscle groups. The afferent process is a reverse process, and the feedback signal comes from the proprioceptors of muscles or joints and the mechanoreceptors of the skin. Based on the complex interaction between the cortex and muscles at different coupling levels, CMC can be roughly divided into linear coupling and nonlinear coupling. Linear coupling analysis methods are mainly based on amplitude squared coherence, short-time Fourier time-frequency coherence, wavelet coherence, Granger causality, partial directed coherence, etc. The nonlinear coupling analysis method is mainly based on nonlinear Granger causality, mutual information, cross-spectral coherence, multispectral phase coherence, transfer entropy estimation, etc.

subsections.subsection_title: Electrophysiological Signatures of Sensorimotor and BOLD Coupling
subsections.content:
Each imaging method has its advantages and disadvantages, and multimodal imaging can complement these advantages to provide a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of changes in brain structure and function. We examined research reports from the last decade and found that the most popular multimodal combinations are EEG-fMRI [ref 1] and EEG-fNIRS. EEG-MEG and fMRI-fNIRS combined studies have also been performed, but few studies have explored motor function assessment after stroke. EEG or MEG and EMG coupling analysis is another popular multimodal analysis method that can establish a correlation between brain activity and muscle behavior, which has unique advantages in assessing motor loss caused by abnormal neural activity after stroke. This section focuses on applying EEG-fMRI coupling, EEG-FNRIS coupling, and EEG-EMG coupling in motor function assessment of stroke.

1) EEG-fMRI Coupling: Simultaneous EEG and fMRI collection can assess the correlation between electrophysiological activity and hemodynamic changes in the brain [ref 1]. Simultaneous resting-state EEG-fMRI and simultaneous taskrelated EEG-fMRI have different meanings and are used in different experimental paradigms. Simultaneous resting-state EEG-fMRI is mainly used to construct brain connectivity networks [ref 1]. In contrast, while simultaneous task-related EEG-fMRI is used primarily to study functional brain activation under specific tasks. The analysis of functional and EC for single-mode signals has been introduced. Multimodal functional network connectivity is a fusion method of EEG and fMRI in network space. The basic steps are as follows: first, spatial independent component analysis is used to extract a functional network from a single mode; then, granger causality analysis is performed on functional networks of EEG and fMRI, respectively, to establish directed connections between networks; finally, the functional networks of EEG and fMRI are matched by network source localization.

Changes in multimodal functional network connectivity in patients after stroke and during rehabilitation, as well as EEG signal-based hemispherical balance analysis described above, can be used to more comprehensively assess motor rehabilitation after stroke. A study evaluating bCI-guided robot-assisted training for stroke rehabilitation showed that the training effect was significantly correlated with FC (derived from fMRI) between ipsilesional M1 and contralesional Bradman area 6. Meanwhile, the training effect significantly correlated with information flow change from contralesional PMA to ipsilesional M1 and from SMA to ipsilesional M1. Related studies from the same team have shown a correlation between increased motor area connectivity and a reduction in interhemispheric asymmetry in the central brain region covering the motor area, both associated with improved FMA scores.

In addition, synchronous EEG-fMRI imaging makes neurofeedback more effective for stroke rehabilitation. Bimodal EEG-fMRI neurofeedback can provide the patient with more information to help him achieve faster and more specific self-regulation. Off-line fMRI analysis revealed that motor activations were stronger under EEG-fMRI neurofeedback than that under single-mode neurofeedback. It is worth emphasizing that EEG-fMRI neurofeedback has the potential to induce an augmented activation of ipsilesional motor areas.

2) EEG-fNIRS Coupling: As mentioned above, both EEG and fMRI signals are susceptible to motion artifacts, and a combination of EEG and fNIRS is an excellent solution to overcome this limitation. Simultaneously EEG-fNIRS can provide comprehensive brain electrical and hemodynamic images. The development of wearable, integrated EEG-fNIRS technology became the basis for multimodal assessment of brain function. An fNIRS-informed EEG source imaging method was used to assess cortical activity and FC. The results showed that task-evoked theta strength in the ipsilesional primary somatosensory was significantly lower in stroke patients than in healthy controls. After four weeks of rehabilitation, with better motor function recovery, the ipsilesional PMC theta strength increased, and the connection between bilateral M1 was strengthened. Asymmetrical indicators based on EEG-fNIRS are commonly used to assess the progression of motor function rehabilitation in stroke patients. Interhemispheric sample entropy and interhemispheric oxygenated hemoglobin were extracted and compared, and significant differences were observed between stroke patients and healthy controls. Simultaneously EEG-fNIRS analysis focusing on EEG-derived event-related desynchronization and oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin concentrations provide a new basis for evaluating neurofeedback training effect. Muchmore, EEG-fNIRS-based assessment of tDCS on stroke rehabilitation has also been widely used, which will be discussed in the next section.

There is a certain degree of information transmission and interaction between the cerebral cortex and the muscles during limb motion. Corticomuscular coupling (CMC) is a quantitative assessment method that can reflect cerebral cortex information and motor muscle state. CMC reveals the FC between the cerebral cortex and muscles by quantifying the synchronization between EMG and EEG, or MEG. The CMC phenomenon between the central nervous system and the periphery nervous system is essential for the neural control of movement. This functional coupling between the brain and muscle originates from the neural signal afferent and efferent process. The brain transmits control commands to the peripheral nervous system in electrical charges through interconnected synapses and neuronal cells and then controls the contraction or extension of various muscle groups. The afferent process is a reverse process, and the feedback signal comes from the proprioceptors of muscles or joints and the mechanoreceptors of the skin. Based on the complex interaction between the cortex and muscles at different coupling levels, CMC can be roughly divided into linear coupling and nonlinear coupling. Linear coupling analysis methods are mainly based on amplitude squared coherence, short-time Fourier time-frequency coherence, wavelet coherence, Granger causality, partial directed coherence, etc. The nonlinear coupling analysis method is mainly based on nonlinear Granger causality, mutual information, cross-spectral coherence, multispectral phase coherence, transfer entropy estimation, etc.

Coherence and mutual information are two basic methods of CMC, and the other methods are extensions of these two methods. Coherence-based CMC linearly evaluates the information interaction between the brain and innervating muscles and is currently the most widely used classical linear coupling analysis method. Coherence-based CMC is essentially calculating the correlation in the frequency domain. The calculation formula is as follows:

where P XY (f ) is the cross-spectrum density of EMG and EEG, P XX (f ) and P YY (f ) are the auto-power spectral density of EMG and EEG, respectively. The value range of CMC is 0 to 1, approaching 1 indicates high interdependence. Coherencebased CMC can analyze the control of the nerve signals of stroke patients on the muscle state under a specific movement paradigm from the time series and quantify the degree of rehabilitation of their motor function. Generally, cerebral injury and muscle atrophy after stroke significantly decrease in CMC values and CMC increases during motor recovery. In addition, the amplitude of CMC on the contralesional of stroke patients was significantly higher than that on the ipsilesional, both in the acute stage and the post-acute stage. Beta and gamma band CMC can best reflect the dynamic changes of the motor system in stroke patients during rehabilitation. More specific studies indicate that the beta band CMC correlates with static force output and the gamma band CMC correlates with dynamic force output. Symmetry degree between contralesional CMC and ipsilesional CMC can also be used to assess stroke severity and recovery progress. Belardinelli et al. tested the CMC value of eight stroke patients before and after four weeks of upper limb exercise rehabilitation, and all patients had a significant increase in beta band CMC. Mutual Information is a measure of the amount of information that a random variable contains another random variable [ref 2]. Suppose the joint distribution of two random variables (X, Y) is p(x, y), the marginal distribution is p(x) and p(y), and the mutual information I(X, Y) is the joint distribution and marginal distribution Relative entropy defined as follows [ref 2]:

Jin et al. proposed a model-free method based on time delay mutual information (TDMI) linear and nonlinear information flow, which can simultaneously detect the linear and nonlinear information components from the cortex to the muscle. Moreover, this method can also determine the flow of information. The difference NI(X, Y) between TDMI(X, Y) and TDMI(Y, X) represents the net flow of information, which can be interpreted as the flow of information between them [ref 2].

If NI(X, Y) is positive, information flows from X to Y; if NI(X, Y) is negative, information flows from Y to X. The calculation formula is as follows:

Transfer entropy is a coupling analysis method based on mutual information, which has advantages in judging information flow and has been favored by researchers in recent years [ref 2]. The transfer spectrum entropy can reveal the coupling state between two signals in the local frequency band. Directed coherence is also a directional coupling analysis method that is often used in studies to explore whether the brain sends information to or receives feedback from the muscles. Although CMC is a relatively new research direction, good results have been obtained, and more studies are needed to evaluate its clinical effects in the future.

Belardinelli et al. tested the CMC value of eight stroke patients before and after four weeks of upper limb exercise rehabilitation, and all patients had a significant increase in beta band CMC. Transfer entropy is a coupling analysis method based on mutual information, which has advantages in judging information flow and has been favored by researchers in recent years ref [65]. The transfer spectrum entropy can reveal the coupling state between two signals in the local frequency band. Directed coherence is also a directional coupling analysis method that is often used in studies to explore whether the brain sends information to or receives feedback from the muscles ref [65]. Although CMC is a relatively new research direction, good results have been obtained, and more studies are needed to evaluate its clinical effects in the future.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Approaches and Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Core Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Modalities in Stroke Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
Brain stimulation has evolved from invasive electrode stimulation to implantable and noninvasive stimulation ref [68], ref [70]. In recent years, with the development of noninvasive brain stimulation ref [68], ref [70], the clinical application of TMS ref [66], and tDCS ref [67], ref [69] has achieved good results in the stroke motor rehabilitation ref [66], ref [67], ref [68], ref [69], ref [70]. The mechanism of how TMS and tDCS contribute to stroke motor rehabilitation has yet to be confirmed ref [66], ref [67], ref [68]. Feasible mechanisms include hemispheric interaction inhibition ref [66], ref [68], ref [70], change of neuronal membrane potential polarity ref [67], ref [69] and brain plasticity ref [66], ref [67], ref [68], ref [69], ref [70]. The TMS and tDCS affect not only the target areas of the motor cortex but also affect the networks of the brain and spinal cord that are connected at a distance ref [66], ref [67], ref [68]. Typical tDCS and TMS devices are shown in Fig. 4. In this section, we will review the research on the application and mechanism of TMS and tDCS in stroke motor rehabilitation within the last ten years.

Brain stimulation has been proved to be effective in the rehabilitation of motor function after stroke ref [66], ref [67], ref [68], ref [69], ref [70]. However, most brain stimulation methods are open loop, requiring the physician to close the loop through the stimulation parameters and the patient's behavioral outcome. Some studies combine brain stimulation with brain imaging to achieve controlled regulation of brain activity. Brain stimulation enables temporal and spatial alterations in brain networks, and brain imaging assesses functional implications resulting from these alterations ref [68], ref [70]. Through the combination, the interaction between different components of the brain network and their respective functional role can be explored, so as to form a more detailed evaluation of brain functional network ref [68]. Some studies have also combined TMS with EEG, fMRI and other imaging techniques to monitor brain activity with higher temporal and spatial resolution, so as to realize the prediction of motor recovery after stroke ref [66], ref [68]. The common use of EEG cap provides a basis for the study of EEG combined with tDCS. The immediate and after effects of tDCS were demonstrated by changes in the characteristics of CMC and EEG signals ref [67], ref [69].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Approaches and Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: rTMS Protocols and Clinical Evidence for Motor Recovery
subsections.content: TMS is painless stimulation of the cerebral cortex or peripheral nerves divided into single-pulse TMS and repetitive TMS (rTMS) ref [1]. Single-pulse TMS is usually used in combination with other imaging methods to assess motor function after stroke, while rTMS is used for motor rehabilitation treatment ref [1]ref [8]. The magnetic field passes unattenuated through high-impedance tissues, such as the skull and scalp, causing the cerebral cortex to generate induced currents ref [1]ref [8]. Induced currents change the membrane potential of cells, increasing or inhibiting the excitability of neurons. Changes in neuronal excitability can affect synaptic plasticity and promote motor learning and motor function recovery after stroke ref [1]ref [5]ref [6]ref [10]ref [11]. According to the size of stimulus frequency, rTMS can be divided into low-frequency stimulation (≤ 1 Hz) and highfrequency stimulation (> 1 Hz) ref [1]ref [3]ref [9]. Low-frequency rTMS can reduce the excitability of the target cortex, while highfrequency rTMS can improve it ref [1]ref [3]ref [4]ref [9]ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Approaches and Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: tDCS Applications, Parameters, and Functional Outcomes
subsections.content: Current studies generally believe that the mechanism of rTMS for stroke rehabilitation is reflected in the modulation of hemispheric interaction [ref 6, ref 8] and enhancement of brain plasticity [ref 4, ref 8]. It has been shown in the previous section that stroke can lead to disruption of the activation balance between the cerebral hemispheres [ref 6, ref 8]. The excitability of the motion-related areas on the ipsilesional hemisphere decreased, but the contralesional hemisphere's excitability increased [ref 6, ref 8]. In addition, when the affected hand performed motor tasks, the contralesional hemisphere inhibited the ipsilesional hemisphere [ref 6, ref 8]. High-frequency TMS can improve the excitability of the motor cortex of the ipsilesional, but low-frequency TMS can inhibit the excitability of the motor cortex of the contralesional, thus realizing the regulation of cerebral hemisphere interaction [ref 7, ref 8]. After treatment with rTMS, the lateralization of power spectral density and information transmission efficiency between bilateral hemispheric central cortexes was significantly changed. In other words, rTMS can modulate hemispheric lateralization, which may be an important neural mechanism to improve motor function [ref 2, ref 3, ref 5].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Approaches and Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanisms of Action: Neuroplasticity, Interhemispheric Balance, and Network Effects
subsections.content: tDCS is a type of transcranial electrical stimulation that regulates the excitability of neurons by applying a weak direct current to the cerebral cortex [ref 4, ref 1]. tDCS can be divided into anodal tDCS and cathodal tDCS according to the polarity of the electrodes applied to the target stimulated brain region. In general, anodal tDCS can enhance the excitability of the target area, while cathodal tDCS can inhibit it [ref 4, ref 2, ref 3]. The current ranging from 0.5 to 2 mA poses no risk to the human body, with a single session lasting from 7 to 40 min [ref 4]. Common electrode pads are 15-35 cm 2 in size, so the current density is about 0.04-0.06 mA/cm 2 [ref 4]. Typically, the moderating effects of tDCS last from a few minutes to several hours after the stimulation [ref 4, ref 8, ref 1, ref 6]. After a single session of 20-30 min, the effect can last about 90 min [ref 4]. After five consecutive days of stimulation, the aftereffect lasted for three months [ref 5, ref 3]. Compared to rTMS, tDCS is more portable and safe, with less patient discomfort, and can be easily combined with other peripheral therapies [ref 1, ref 6, ref 7].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Approaches and Mechanisms
subsections.subsection_title: Trial Design, Combination Strategies, and Broader Context
subsections.content: Rehabilitation: tDCS has been increasingly used as an adjunct therapy for motor rehabilitation, but its potential application is limited because of the unclear mechanism of action ref [3]. The current explanation for the means of tDCS can be summarized as changing the polarity of neuronal membrane potential and regulating synaptic plasticity ref [3]. The underlying mechanism of tDCS has been studied since the 1960s, and it was proved that tDCS could change cortical excitability by detecting the change of motor-evoked potential through TMS in 1998 ref [3]. When weak direct current is applied to the scalp, the resting membrane potential and spontaneous discharge rate of neurons are modulated, leading to plasticity ref [3]. Anodal tDCS causes neurons membrane to depolarize, leading to an increase in the excitability of the cortex, while cathodal tDCS causes neurons membrane to polarize to decrease excitability ref [3]. The membrane potential polarization state change may be the mechanism of effect after tDCS. TDCS can induce long-lasting changes in synaptic excitability in the motor cortex, and the biological agent is LTP and LTD phenomena at the cellular level ref [3]. Some studies suggest that tDCS induces synaptic plasticity by altering changes in neurotransmitter concentration ref [3]. Moreover, some studies have shown that anodic tDCS can reduce gamma-aminobutyric acid in the cortex and enhance cortical excitability. On the contrary, cathode tDCS reduced glutamate concentration and thus reduced cortical excitability ref [3]. Studies have shown that weak tDCS can produce sustained excitability ref [3]. Both anodal and cathodal tDCS increased the affected M1 motor-evoked potential in stroke patients ref [3]. The after effect of tDCS also reflected in reducing the inhibitory effect from CL to IL ref [3]. In addition, changes in dopamine, acetylcholine, and serotonin may also be involved, but more research is needed to confirm this ref [3, 4].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Clinical Perspectives in Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
The use of brain imaging provides a more accurate solution to the precise assessment of motor function post-stroke, which is the basis of navigated rehabilitation ref [101]. To better characterize brain function networks, high spatial, and temporal resolution imaging techniques are required ref [101]. Multimodal imaging can make up for the defect of single mode and will become the mainstream research direction in the future ref [101]. EEG-fMRI and EEG-fNIRS have attracted much attention and obtained some research results, and can further explore their potential in the future. CMC is a novel evaluation method that can get information about muscle states and brain states ref [101]. It provides a correlation between the brain and muscles (which reflects the brain's ability to control muscles) and provides time delay information (which reflects changes in information transmission), which is helpful for assessing motor function after stroke ref [101]. Graph theory can supplement traditional statistical analysis and is very important for building brain networks ref [101]. A number of features can be extracted that are more indicative of change before and after treatment, which are essential for quantifying recovery progress ref [101]. The evaluation method based on brain imaging can well supplement the deficiency of the clinical qualitative evaluation scale ref [101].

Exercise rehabilitation after stroke is affected by sociodemographic characteristics (such as age, gender, race, etc.), clinical factors (such as stroke type, co-morbidities, rehabilitation therapeutics, etc.), and genetic factors ref [219]. As a result, there is a significant difference in stroke patients, which requires the establishment of individualized rehabilitation therapies. More effective than scale assessment, brain imaging technology can be used to establish the state of the individual brain functional network for each patient so that personalized brain stimulation rehabilitation therapy can be built ref [101]. Fatigue is a common syndrome after stroke, which will directly affect the results of motor function assessment and intervention. Fatigue manifestations in stroke patients include brain fatigue and muscle fatigue. Taking fatigue into account when constructing a patient's brain functional network is a grand challenge, as in brain stimulation treatment. The assessment and treatment of post-stroke fatigue have attracted the attention of researchers, and brain imaging and brain stimulation techniques can also become effective means ref [99] ref [100].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Clinical Perspectives in Rehabilitation
subsections.content: Although rTMS and tDCS are effective in rebuilding motor function post-stroke, there are no guidelines for clinical use. The safe range of brain stimulation parameters should pay attention, which is crucial to whether patients accept treatment. Effective stimulation processes and paradigms need to be explored, which is the focus of current research. Brain stimulation combined with other interventions proved to be more effective and more acceptable to stroke patients. Combined augmented reality-based training can significantly increase muscle activity and strength of chronic phase stroke patients compared to EMG-triggered functional electric stimulation alone ref [213]. Functional electric stimulation and roboticassisted training can achieve shoulder, elbow, and wrist complex upper limb movements ref [214]. The study preliminarily proved that bilateral tDCS to robot-assisted therapy have significant rehabilitation effects on stroke patients, and there are significant differences in patients with different stroke stages and types ref [102]. Vision restoration training combined with tDCS may be better than standard vision training for rehabilitation, but this conclusion needs further proof ref [103]. Brain stimulation improves brain plasticity more than traditional physical training, but the combination of the two is more effective in restoring brain and muscle function ref [102] ref [103].

subsections.section_title: Future Directions and Clinical Perspectives in Rehabilitation
subsections.content: This article emphasizes the importance of assessment for rehabilitation, and the combination of noninvasive brain imaging and brain stimulation is the future direction. After an accurate assessment of the cerebral functional network, hemispheric balance index, and CMC characteristic values of stroke patients, the brain stimulation paradigm formulation can improve rehabilitation efficiency and make the therapy closeloop. A simultaneous tDCS-EEG study demonstrated that tDCS can modulate the synchronization of cortical rhythms during and after administration ref [211] ref [96]. Simultaneous use of tDCS and EEG-EMG system demonstrated that stroke patients had the greatest changes in CMC under anode tDCS, with the greatest effect occurring 10-min after stimulation ref [212]. The efficacy of rTMS was evaluated by fMRI and the results were consistent with the clinical evaluation ref [217] ref [104]. Researchers used rTMS in combination with EEG-EMG system demonstrated that rTMS can improve motor function by constructing a brainmuscle network, which providing us with a new research perspective ref [218]. Closed-loop studies of neuromodulationbased rehabilitation methods can explore safe and effective stimulus parameters to promote their use in clinical rehabilitation. Due to the limitation of equipment and experimental conditions, the combined research of some brain imaging and brain stimulation methods has not formed a closed loop. However, this should be the focus of future research.

This article summarizes state of art in brain imaging and stimulation, exploring potential solutions to post-stroke motor rehabilitation. The principle, advantages, limitations, and analytical methods of EEG, MEG, fMRI, and fNIRS brain imaging were presented with the intent of demonstrating the benefits of brain imaging in the motor function assessment of stroke ref [118], ref [24], ref [30], ref [74], ref [79], ref [84], ref [89], ref [100]. We summarized the application of rTMS and tDCS in stroke rehabilitation, the setting of stimulus parameters, and their mechanism ref [124], ref [129], ref [137], ref [146], ref [154], ref [162]. More studies are needed in the future to demonstrate its effectiveness in motor rehabilitation and to identify clinical stimulation paradigms ref [129], ref [146], ref [162]. Finally, we discussed the prospects of combining brain imaging with brain stimulation in stroke rehabilitation, which we believe will be the direction of future research ref [176], ref [184], ref [191]. Based on the summary of motor rehabilitation of stroke, there are typical problems in motor impairment caused by neurological diseases, such as spinal injury and epilepsy. It is expected that this article would facilitate researchers and practitioners with a better understanding of noninvasive brain imaging and brain stimulation and their development on solutions to post-stroke motor rehabilitation.
